questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: My main motivation for choosing Tokyo, and Japan in general was the opportunity to gain international academic experience in a country with a culture very different from my own. I felt that living in Japan would give me valuable new perspectives, as I had never been to East Asia before.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was not very easy, as only a limited number of people spoke English, which made practical tasks such as registering my address and arranging insurance quite challenging. However, everything related to the university itself—such as the admission procedure and course registration—was more straightforward. The staff at the International Students Office were very helpful and always willing to answer questions, which made the process much smoother once I knew where to turn for assistance.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was assigned a tutor who helped me with many of the practical matters, such as registration procedures, and who was available to answer various questions during my first weeks. The International Students Office was also very supportive and always ready to clarify the things my tutor could not assist with. In addition, the dormitory where I stayed (Mejirodai) had very kind and helpful staff who provided guidance on everyday matters.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was incredibly easy. I simply applied through the university and was assigned a place at Mejirodai International Village, which is the closest housing option to Hongo Campus. I would highly recommend this dorm to anyone going on exchange to UTokyo, especially if they will be studying at Hongo. The dorm is new and clean, located in a pleasant residential neighborhood, filled with international students, and offers a very convenient and comfortable living environment.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Do not live alone if you can avoid it. Choosing to live in a dorm allows you to be much closer to other students and to take part in the social environment. Living together with other international students means you always have people around to share experiences with. During my stay, I did not eat dinner alone a single night—there was always someone to share a meal with. 

From a practical perspective, commuting was also very manageable. From Mejirodai International Village, it took me about 30 minutes to get to Hongo Campus—I would walk to Myogadani Station and then take the train directly to Hongo.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration process was a bit confusing at first, as the Academic Affairs System (UTAS – similar to KUnet) is not very intuitive and takes some time to get used to. Fortunately, I had a tutor who guided me through the steps and answered my questions regarding both the initial admission procedure and the course registration. In addition, there were several orientation sessions for international students where we received detailed information about the registration procedure, course options, and other practical matters. The orientation for my specific graduate school, however, was conducted in Japanese with a translator present, which made it a bit difficult to follow everything in detail.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Both my assigned tutor and the International Student Office were of great help throughout the semester.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I was able to register for all the courses I wanted without any major problems. The process is done directly through UTAS as soon as the course registration period opens. During the first week of the semester, you also have the opportunity to “trial” classes, which you can later drop if you did not like them during the first week.

One important thing to be aware of, however, is the language requirement. If you are not comfortable speaking Japanese, it is best to choose courses labeled only as “English” rather than those listed as “English/Japanese.”

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Consider the workload of every course you take, as it can vary significantly depending on the professor and the type of class. 

During the course registration week, take advantage of the opportunity to try out as many classes as possible. This will give you a better sense of the teaching style, workload, and content before you decide which ones to keep.

I would also recommend trying to keep Fridays free if possible. Having a three-day weekend made it much easier for me to go on longer trips around Japan and abroad.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The courses were not especially difficult in terms of content, but they required a different academic approach than I was used to. Most of the classes I took were based on jurisprudence and legal research rather than traditional legal dogmatics, which meant that I had to adjust my way of thinking and studying. It took some time to get used to analyzing broader theoretical, comparative and sociological perspectives instead of focusing primarily on the application of legal rules.

The evaluation methods were also quite different from what I had experienced at home. Instead of written exams, assessment was usually based on a final paper or a series of smaller papers submitted throughout the semester. In addition, class participation was an important factor in the overall grade. While this system was not necessarily more difficult, it required more continuous engagement and preparation during the semester.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: All of my classes at UTokyo were seminar-based. The class sizes were noticeably smaller, which created a more interactive atmosphere. Each class also had its own particular style, especially when it came to evaluation methods—some relied on a single final paper, while others required several smaller assignments combined with active participation.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Anglo-American Law (with p. Masayuki Tamaruya), Sociology of Law (with p. Dimitri Vanoverbeke), Comparative Law (with p. Carol Lawson), International Commercial Law and Negotiation Strategy (with p. Masayuki Tamaruya). 8 credits in total. Very competent and friendly professors. Highly recommend these courses.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would honestly recommend all of the courses I took, as each of them offered valuable insights and perspectives that I would not have encountered at home. Taken together, however, the workload was heavier than I initially expected—across my classes I ended up writing roughly 13,000 words in papers.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
In general, Japan turned out to be noticeably less expensive than Denmark, but this really depends on the category of spending. Everyday items such as food and drinks were often cheaper. Public transportation can add up, but with a commuter pass (that you can get since you are a student) it becomes more manageable and quite affordable compared to Danish standards.

On the other hand, certain things were more expensive than I expected. Travelling around Japan can quickly become costly and many imported goods that you are used to (like fruit and vegetables) were also surprisingly expensive. Overall, though, the cost of living felt lower than in Denmark, provided you adapt to the local way of doing things.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There were certainly many cultural, athletic, and social activities available, but in my experience most of them required a fairly good command of Japanese in order to fully participate. 

That said, my dormitory organized informal social activities, which made it easier to meet both international and Japanese students.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would strongly recommend travelling and eating out as often as you can.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
In Tokyo itself, you could spend months exploring different neighborhoods. For short trips, I would highly recommend places like Karuizawa, Nikko, Kamakura, Kawagoe, and various nearby mountains such as Mt. Mitake, Mt. Takao or Mt. Fuji.

If you have more time, it is worth exploring Hokkaido and the Kansai region. 

Travelling abroad is also easy, for example Seoul, Hong Kong or Shanghai.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy overall. Of course, there were many differences compared to what I was used to at home, but most of them were positive and simply part of the adventure of living in Japan. Everyday life in Tokyo is very convenient, people are generally extremely polite and helpful, and public transportation makes it easy to get around. While some things—like the language barrier or certain bureaucratic processes—took a bit of getting used to, I never felt that it was overwhelming.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Living in a dorm is definitely the best option, as it places you right at the center of social life and makes it much easier to meet both international and Japanese students. Beyond that, the most important advice is to be open-minded and willing to start conversations with as many people as you can. Joining shared meals, study groups, events, trips and so on is also a good way to build connections.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The language barrier was by far the biggest challenge. Many (in my experience most) Japanese people do not speaking English very well.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: What I appreciated most was the incredible convenience of everyday life in Japan.I was also impressed by the overall cleanliness of the cities and public spaces. Finally, the friendliness and politeness of people stood out.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Don’t let the initial paperwork and practical taskss care you off. It may feel overwhelming at first, but it is absolutely worth the effort once you arrive.

2. Be social and make the most of your time. Say yes to invitations, join group dinners, and spend time with the people around you.

3. Take the initiative. Be the one arranging trips, dinners, gatherings.

4. Use the course registration trial week wisely. Try out as many classes as possible, have strategic days off so you have time for longer travels.

5. Take time to explore Japan beyond Tokyo and explore the rest of Asia as much as possible.

6. Keep in touch with the friends you make at UTokyo.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Nothing in particular that I haven’t already mentioned above.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: For me, the most rewarding aspects were the combination of academic, personal, and cultural experiences. On the academic side, it was a privilege to study at such a highly respected university and to learn from competent professors. On a personal level, I really valued the chance to use English on a daily basis and to interact with people from many different backgrounds. Finally, exploring a culture so different from my own was incredibly enriching.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The biggest challenge for me was finding the right balance between academic responsibilities and social life. In the end it was not overwhelming, and I feel that I managed to find a good rhythm.

questions.answer: Yes
